subject: Suggestion: reorganisation and renaming of colour scales

messages.author: fc22cb727156ff4f
messages.subject: Suggestion: reorganisation and renaming of colour scales
parts:
Hi all,

The gradients scales could be greatly simplified: gradient, gradient2,
gradientn... all this is complex.
Basically, scale_gradient should be the only interface, behave like
scale_gradientn and have a midpoint argument, NULL by default, which,
when specified, makes it behave like scale_gradient2. I thought I read
it was improved in the new version although I cannot see it in the dev
version I have at the moment.

scale_colour_hue is difficult to understand by novice,
non-graphic-oriented users (particularly non-english speaking ones).
What about scale_colour_discrete and scale_colour_continuous, to match
with all the rest of the scales?

Finally, the fact that "colour" affects the inside of objects for
geom_point but the outside for most others is bad for consistency and
hence learning and discovery. What about having separate fill and
stroke for all geoms (with stroke basically replacing colour
currently)? And then have colour do something "intelligent" depending
on the scale (i.e. stroke for path, fill for polygon, fill for tile
etc.). That would give fine, consistent control when needed
(fill/stroke) but also allow a more natural approach ("I want this to
be *coloured* according to that", without having to care what the
colour is applied to). This simpler approach would probably suffice
for the majority of users (very rarely do I use both fill and stroke
colours on the same object).

I understand this would also cause a backward compatibility problem
(using both fill and colour on something where colour would refere to
fill) but again, that would be the price for a better behaviour in the
end.

JiHO
---

messages.author: d34d025a513c07fc
messages.subject: Re: Suggestion: reorganisation and renaming of colour scales
parts:
On Wed, Jan 18, 2012 at 4:11 PM, JiHO <jo.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi all,

The gradients scales could be greatly simplified: gradient, gradient2,
gradientn... all this is complex.
Basically, scale_gradient should be the only interface, behave like
scale_gradientn and have a midpoint argument, NULL by default, which,
when specified, makes it behave like scale_gradient2. I thought I read
it was improved in the new version although I cannot see it in the dev
version I have at the moment.

I think that to be more consistent across scales, it would be better to have something like this:
scale_colour(type="hue")
scale_colour(type="gradientn")
scale_fill(type="gradient")

This would keep the syntax parallel with your proposed scale_x(), where the part after the "scale_" is the name of the aesthetic. The 'type=' parameter could also be used for other scales. Here's one possibility:
scale_shape(type="hollow")

scale_colour_hue is difficult to understand by novice,
non-graphic-oriented users (particularly non-english speaking ones).
What about scale_colour_discrete and scale_colour_continuous, to match
with all the rest of the scales?

Don't scale_colour_discrete and scale_colour_continuous default to using hue? For example, these both give the same result:

dat <- data.frame(x=LETTERS[1:3], y=3)
ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y, fill=x)) + geom_bar() + scale_fill_discrete()
ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y, fill=x)) + geom_bar() + scale_fill_hue()

I agree that "hue" can be difficult to understand for novices. I also think that it is usually not a good choice, and I almost never use it. This is because lightness is kept constant, making it hard to distinguish differently-colored regions. The hues can often be difficult for colorblind people to distinguish. For example, with three hues, like in the example above, the red and green bars look very similar for those with red-green colorblindness. (I'm using a program called Sim Daltonism on my Mac to simulate what things look like for colorblind people.)

Finally, the fact that "colour" affects the inside of objects for
geom_point but the outside for most others is bad for consistency and
hence learning and discovery. What about having separate fill and
stroke for all geoms (with stroke basically replacing colour
currently)? And then have colour do something "intelligent" depending
on the scale (i.e. stroke for path, fill for polygon, fill for tile
etc.). That would give fine, consistent control when needed
(fill/stroke) but also allow a more natural approach ("I want this to
be *coloured* according to that", without having to care what the
colour is applied to). This simpler approach would probably suffice
for the majority of users (very rarely do I use both fill and stroke
colours on the same object).

The inconsistent meaning of 'colour' can be traced to grid graphics, specifically gpar. If you look at ?gpar, you'll see a 'col' and 'fill' parameter. The 'colour' in ggplot2 gets mapped to 'col', and 'fill' goes to 'fill'. For example, the inconsistency in the shape colour/fill specification can be traced here. The fill-only shapes (15-18) have no outline and use 'col' to refer to the fill color. The hollow shapes (0-14) are only outlines, and 'col' refers to the line color. The fill+outline shapes (21-25) use 'col' to refer to the outline, and 'fill' to refer to the fill.

Side note: It probably wouldn't be too difficult to insulate the user from this inconsistency in color/fill for shapes.

I think it would be best to use something like 'linecolour' instead of 'colour', to always refer to lines, and keep 'fill' to refer to fill colors. Various line properties could be named like this.
- linetype
- linecolour
- linesize (instead of 'size')
- lineend


These changes would definitely break backward compatibility. But it might be worthwhile.

-Winston

If you want to use the scale gradients in that way, just use
scale_gradientn - they are now all implemented with the (mostly) the
same algorithm behind the scenes. But scale_gradient2 is a little
special because it ensures that the gradient is symmetrical around the
midpoint, even if the data are not. I think this behaviour is
different enough to deserve its own name and it would be confusing to
lump into one scale.

> stroke for all geoms (with stroke basically replacing colour

> on the scale (i.e. stroke for path, fill for polygon, fill for tile
> etc.). That would give fine, consistent control when needed

> be *coloured* according to that", without having to care what the
> colour is applied to). This simpler approach would probably suffice

I guess I don't really see the problem here - I just think of points
as being all outside. It would be possible to wrap around the default
R behaviour (which I agree is confusing), but it would require a lot
of extra work, for not much extra gain.

> I understand this would also cause a backward compatibility problem
> (using both fill and colour on something where colour would refere to
> fill) but again, that would be the price for a better behaviour in the
> end.

I think if I did it again I'd use stroke and fill.

> Various line properties could be named like this.
> - linetype
> - linecolour

Isn't "stroke" generic enough. But maybe that is, like hue, a too
technical term.

The drawback to using 'stroke' is that it could mean many things. For example, in a vector illustration program, you can change the following stroke properties: thickness, dashed/dotted, color, etc. It wouldn't be obvious that 'stroke' refers to the color of the stroke, and not the stroke thickness.

> - linesize (instead of 'size')

But size applies to several other things (points, etc.)

I was actually separating it from other kinds of 'size' on purpose, because the size of a point is different from the thickness of a line. (There are many times where I've wanted to control the thickness of point outlines, but there's presently no such option in ggplot2.)

-Winston

dat <- data.frame(x=LETTERS[1:5], y=1:5)
